procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 19.12.2017 of the High Court of M.P. Principal Seat at Jabalpur in CRA No.193 of 2006
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellant filed a Criminal Appeal (CRA No. 193 of 2006) before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur challenging his conviction and sentence under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, which was awarded by the Trial Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal on 19.12.2017.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant approached the Supreme Court by filing Criminal Appeal No. 2806 of 2024, challenging the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

directions: If the Appellant is on bail, his bail bonds are cancelled, and he is directed to surrender and undergo the remainder of the sentence.
If the Appellant is already in custody, in that event, he shall complete the remainder of the sentence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the courts below erred in not appreciating the contradictions or discrepancies which would dislodge the prosecution’s case.

facts: The appellant argued that the prosecution's case contained inherent contradictions and discrepancies.

Specific issues raised included inconsistencies in eyewitness testimonies, deficiencies in the recording of the FIR, and the Investigating Officer's failure to mark the incident spot on the site plan.
law: When eyewitness testimonies are consistent, unimpeachable, and corroborated by medical evidence or the recovery of a weapon, deficiencies in the FIR alone are not a valid ground to overturn a conviction.
The unfiltered testimony of a rustic witness, even if it has minor inconsistencies, should not be discarded and must be evaluated comprehensively.
It is unreasonable to expect a witness to recall every minute detail of an occurrence with perfect accuracy unless they have been coached.
application: The Court found the testimonies of the eyewitnesses to be consistent, unimpeachable, and duly corroborated by medical evidence and the recovery of the weapon.

It held that any discrepancies in the witness statements were minor and did not undermine the core of their testimony, noting that such inconsistencies are natural for a witness who has not been coached.
The Court found no evidence of ulterior motives or fabrication on the part of the Investigating Officer.

Given the strength of the corroborated eyewitness accounts, the Court determined that the alleged deficiencies in the FIR and other procedural aspects were not significant enough to undermine the prosecution's case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there were no contradictions or discrepancies in the prosecution's case significant enough to warrant overturning the conviction. The Court found the eyewitness testimony to be strong, consistent, and corroborated, and dismissed the appellant's arguments as being without merit. Therefore, the lower courts did not err in their appreciation of the evidence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the presence of the appellant at the place of occurrence was doubtful.

facts: The incident occurred at 9:30 pm on a summer night at a location adjacent to the complainant's home.
The appellant argued that visibility was poor due to darkness and that the complainant (P.W.10) was not well-acquainted with him, making identification doubtful.
Eyewitnesses, who were familiar with the appellant, identified him as being present and participating in the crime.
The appellant's name was mentioned in the initial report, which was recorded less than two hours after the occurrence.
The appellant did not raise a plea of alibi in his statement under Section 313 CrPC, nor did he cross-examine witnesses on this point or provide any evidence to support such a defense.
law: A person who pleads alibi in contrast to an eyewitness version has a 'cumbrous onus' (heavy burden) to prove their absence from the scene and time of the crime.
application: The Court dismissed the argument of poor visibility, reasoning that a summer night would have minimal obstruction to visibility for the witnesses.

The Court found the eyewitness identification credible because the crime scene was adjacent to the complainant's home, making it easier for witnesses to observe, and the witnesses were already familiar with the appellant.
The Court placed significant weight on the appellant's failure to raise or prove a plea of alibi. This failure weakened his claim that he was not present.

The Court found no evidence of a motive for the witnesses to falsely implicate the appellant, noting that his name surfaced in the very first version of the events recorded shortly after the incident.
The Court concluded that the eyewitness testimonies were consistent and unimpeachable, providing a solid basis to affirm the appellant's presence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim that his presence at the scene was doubtful. It found the eyewitness testimony credible due to the witnesses' familiarity with the appellant and their proximity to the scene. The Court heavily relied on the appellant's failure to raise or provide any evidence for a plea of alibi, concluding there was no reason to doubt he was present and actively participated in the crime.

issue.issue_text: Whether deficiencies in the recording of the FIR, such as not reading its contents to the complainant, constitute a valid ground to overturn the conviction when eyewitness testimonies are consistent and corroborated.

facts: The complainant, during cross-examination, claimed that the First Information Report (FIR) was not read out to her before she put her thumb impression on it.
The prosecution's case was supported by eyewitness testimonies that were found to be consistent and unimpeachable.
This eyewitness testimony was further corroborated by medical evidence and the recovery of the weapon used in the crime.
law: An FIR is not a substantive piece of evidence; its primary purpose is to start an investigation and it can only be used to corroborate or contradict the informant's testimony.
Procedural requirements for recording an FIR, such as reading it over to the informant, are not obligatory to the extent that their omission would automatically invalidate the prosecution's case.
Deficiencies in the recording of an FIR alone do not constitute a valid ground to overturn a conviction when the prosecution's case is otherwise strong.
To challenge a conviction based on such a deficiency, the accused must demonstrate that the omission caused them actual prejudice, hindering their ability to mount an effective defense.
application: The Court applied the principle that strong, corroborated evidence outweighs minor procedural flaws.
It found that the consistent testimonies of the eyewitnesses, supported by medical evidence and the recovery of the weapon, formed a solid basis for the conviction.
The Court then considered whether the alleged failure to read the FIR to the complainant caused any prejudice to the appellant (the accused).

It concluded that no prejudice was demonstrated. The appellant had received a copy of the FIR and the charge sheet, was able to cross-examine the informant effectively, and did not offer a substantial defense beyond a vague denial. Therefore, the procedural lapse did not impact the fairness of the trial or the outcome of the case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that deficiencies in the recording of an FIR, such as not reading its contents to the complainant, are not a valid ground to overturn a conviction when the case is supported by consistent, unimpeachable, and corroborated eyewitness testimony. The Court found the procedural flaw to be insignificant in the face of strong evidence and the appellant's failure to show any resulting prejudice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the disclosure statement by the appellant leading to the discovery and seizure of the knife was admissible in evidence.

facts: After being apprehended and while in police custody, the appellant made a disclosure statement (Ex.P.14) to the Investigating Officer (P.W.14).
The statement was made voluntarily and was witnessed by Lallu Vishwakarma (P.W.11).
The statement revealed the location of a concealed knife, which was the weapon of offence.
This disclosure directly led to the discovery and subsequent seizure of the knife.
The testimony of the Investigating Officer regarding the recovery was supported by the witness (P.W.11).
law: Under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act (IEA), a statement made by an accused person while in police custody is admissible if it leads to the discovery of a new fact.
application: The Court examined whether the disclosure statement was made voluntarily or was secured through coercion, treating it as a question of fact.
Based on the testimonies of the Investigating Officer (P.W.14) and the witness (P.W.11), the Court was satisfied that the appellant made the statement voluntarily.
The Court found that the statement directly resulted in the discovery and recovery of the knife, a relevant fact in the case.
Therefore, the Court concluded that the disclosure statement fulfilled the basic requirements of Section 27 of the IEA.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the disclosure statement made by the appellant, to the extent that it led to the recovery of the knife, was correctly admitted in evidence as an incriminating material against him.

issue.issue_text: Whether the absence of blood group classification or inconclusive FSL results on the recovered weapon would affect the prosecution case.

facts: A knife was recovered based on a disclosure statement made by the appellant.
A Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) report confirmed the presence of human blood on this knife.
However, the FSL test to determine the blood group was inconclusive.
Other weapons connected to the case were also tested, but human blood was found only on the knife recovered from the appellant.
The appellant did not provide any explanation for the presence of human blood on the knife.
law: The presence of human blood on a weapon recovered at the instance of an accused is an important piece of evidence.
It is the responsibility of the accused to provide an explanation for the presence of human blood on the weapon of the crime.
An accused's failure or 'conspicuous silence' in explaining the presence of human blood is a circumstance that can be held against them and lends support to the prosecution's case.
application: The Court acknowledged that the blood group test was inconclusive.
However, it emphasized that the FSL report did positively identify human blood on the knife recovered from the appellant.
The Court found it significant that among all the weapons tested, only the appellant's knife had human blood on it.
The Court then placed the burden on the appellant to explain this incriminating finding.
Since the appellant failed to offer any explanation, the Court treated his silence as a factor that strengthened the prosecution's argument.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that the inconclusive blood group result did not harm the prosecution's case. The confirmed presence of unexplained human blood on the weapon recovered from the appellant was a significant incriminating circumstance that supported the prosecution's case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the mere non-obtainment of a medical fitness certificate would deter the court from considering a properly recorded statement under Section 161 CrPC as a dying declaration.

facts: A statement from a person, Tularam, who later died, was recorded by an investigating officer under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).

The defense argued that this statement could not be considered a 'dying declaration' because the investigating officer did not obtain a certificate from a doctor confirming Tularam's mental fitness to make the statement.
The statement was recorded a day after the incident, and the declarant clearly explained the incident and specified the role of the appellant.
The injuries found during the post-mortem examination corroborated the deceased's statement.
law: A statement recorded by a police officer under Section 161 CrPC can be treated as a dying declaration under Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act, due to an exception carved out in Section 162(2) of the CrPC.
The requirement of a doctor's certification regarding the mental fitness of the declarant is not a rigid rule but a 'rule of caution' or a matter of prudence.
The ultimate responsibility rests with the court to ensure that the declarant was in a sound state of mind when making the statement.

If the court is satisfied that the declaration is voluntary and truthful, it can be acted upon even without a doctor's certificate. Eyewitness testimony or the content of the statement itself can establish the declarant's fitness.
application: The Court first affirmed that a statement recorded under Section 161 CrPC is legally admissible as a dying declaration.
Addressing the absence of a medical certificate, the Court reiterated that this is not a fatal flaw. The key is for the court to be satisfied about the declarant's mental state.

The Court examined the content of the statement itself and found that the declarant had not only properly explained the incident but had also clearly specified the appellant's role. This internal evidence demonstrated that the declarant was in a fit condition and sound state of mind.
Furthermore, the court noted that the statement was corroborated by the medical evidence from the post-mortem examination, which enhanced its credibility.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the mere non-obtainment of a medical fitness certificate does not deter the court from considering a properly recorded statement under Section 161 CrPC as a dying declaration. The court can determine the declarant's fitness from other evidence, including the clarity and coherence of the statement itself.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the courts below erred in not appreciating the contradictions or discrepancies which would dislodge the prosecution’s case.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that there were contradictions and discrepancies in the testimonies of the eyewitnesses, which the lower courts failed to appreciate, and these were significant enough to make the prosecution's case unreliable.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the judgment did not warrant interference. The eyewitnesses were illiterate labourers, and their testimonies, even with minor inconsistencies expected after a lapse of time, should not be discarded. Their evidence should be evaluated comprehensively, especially as they denied being tutored.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the presence of the appellant at the place of occurrence was doubtful.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that his presence at the scene of the crime was not proven beyond a reasonable doubt.
respondent_arguments: The respondent relied on eyewitness testimony which established the appellant's presence. One eyewitness deposed that she knew the accused who were present in court, a group that indisputably included the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether deficiencies in the recording of the FIR, such as not reading its contents to the complainant, constitute a valid ground to overturn the conviction when eyewitness testimonies are consistent and corroborated.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that procedural deficiencies in the recording of the FIR were a serious flaw that should invalidate the conviction.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the conviction was based on strong, consistent, and corroborated eyewitness testimonies, which outweigh any minor procedural deficiencies in the FIR.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the disclosure statement by the appellant leading to the discovery and seizure of the knife was admissible in evidence.
appellant_arguments: The appellant challenged the admissibility of the disclosure statement leading to the recovery of the knife and also submitted that the knife injury was not caused by him.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the disclosure statement was correctly admitted in evidence as it led to the discovery of a relevant fact, namely the weapon (knife).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the absence of blood group classification or inconclusive FSL results on the recovered weapon would affect the prosecution case.
appellant_arguments: The appellant likely argued that the lack of conclusive forensic evidence, such as blood group matching on the weapon, created reasonable doubt and failed to link the weapon to the crime.
respondent_arguments: The respondent likely argued that the absence of corroborative forensic evidence is not fatal to the case when there is sufficient and credible direct evidence from eyewitnesses.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the mere non-obtainment of a medical fitness certificate would deter the court from considering a properly recorded statement under Section 161 CrPC as a dying declaration.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that a statement cannot be treated as a valid dying declaration without a medical certificate confirming the declarant was in a fit state of mind to make it.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that a medical fitness certificate is a rule of caution, not a mandatory requirement, and its absence does not automatically invalidate a dying declaration if the court is otherwise satisfied of the declarant's fitness.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: For information received from an accused person to be proved, there must be a discovery of a fact in consequence of that information, and only that portion of the information which relates distinctly to the fact discovered is admissible. Furthermore, Section 161 empowers the Police to orally examine any person who is acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case.
obiter: In our quest to find out whether the Appellant is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt, we have expanded the wings of our limited jurisdiction and assumed the role akin to that of the 1st Appellate Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: After expanding its jurisdiction to re-examine the evidence akin to a first appellate court, the Court found that the prosecution's case, primarily resting on eyewitness testimony, was credible and sufficient to prove the appellant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The Court held that eyewitness statements must be appreciated in their entirety, not in piecemeal, and that minor discrepancies do not discredit an otherwise consistent narrative. This core testimony, supported by the admissible discovery of the weapon based on the appellant's disclosure, was sufficient to uphold the conviction.
legal_tests_applied: For a disclosure statement leading to a discovery to be admissible, the court applied the two-pronged test from Laxman v. State of Maharashtra: (i) There should be a discovery of the fact. (ii) The discovery of fact should be in consequence of information received from a person accused of an offence.
When evaluating eyewitness testimony, the statement has to be read and appreciated in its entirety and not in piecemeal.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument regarding contradictions in eyewitness testimony failed because the court adopted the principle that such testimony must be read as a whole, not dissected for minor inconsistencies.

The challenge to the appellant's presence at the scene was rejected as the court found it 'too far-fetched to dissect Usha Bai’s version to hold that the Appellant was not present or participated in the occurrence' after considering her statement in its entirety.

The appellant's challenge to the admissibility of the disclosure statement leading to the recovery of the knife was unsuccessful as it met the authoritative two-part legal test for discovery of a fact based on information from an accused.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution's case succeeded because the court found the eyewitness testimony of Usha Bai (P.W.10) to be credible when 'read and appreciated in its entirety and not in piecemeal'.

The disclosure statement leading to the discovery of the knife was held to be admissible evidence as it satisfied the established legal test that the discovery of a fact was in consequence of information received from the accused.

The concurrent findings of the Trial Court and the High Court, which accepted the prosecution's version, were affirmed after the Supreme Court conducted its own thorough re-examination of the evidence.
policy_considerations: In its 'quest to find out whether the Appellant is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt,' the Court consciously 'expanded the wings of our limited jurisdiction and assumed the role akin to that of the 1st Appellate Court,' indicating a policy of ensuring a thorough and substantive review of evidence to prevent any miscarriage of justice, even where jurisdiction is typically limited.
